The instrument is a chordophone, used mainly in Carnatic music, and today it is mostly found in South India. A beginner can first get to know the arrangement of six main melody strings, three drone strings and eleven or twelve sympathetic strings, then practise coordinating the right-hand picking with the left-hand slide; its tuning is similar to that of the sitar and the Saraswati veena, but the arrangement of the main strings is different.

葛圖瓦賈姆琴主要作為卡納提克音樂中的獨奏樂器出現，亦見於世界音樂合作音樂會，以及: The gottuvadyam appears mainly as a solo instrument in Carnatic music, and also in world-music collaboration concerts and in North–South Indian duet line-ups. Its performing occasions are mostly modern South Indian concerts, and it has also been associated with court music traditions; when listening, notice that it is a fretless chordophone whose pitch is changed with a slide, and the melodic line woven from the main strings, the drone strings and the sympathetic strings.
葛圖瓦賈姆琴又稱齊特拉維納，是南印度卡納提克音樂中的無品魯特式維納，屬弦鳴樂器。: The gottuvadyam, also called the chitra veena, is the fretless lute-type veena of South Indian Carnatic music and belongs to the chordophones. In its modern form, like the South Indian veena, it has six main melody strings, three drone strings and eleven or twelve sympathetic strings. The right hand plucks the metal melody strings with a pick, while the left hand slides a cylindrical slide of hardwood, buffalo horn, glass, steel or Teflon along the strings to change the pitch. It is used mainly for solos, and also in world-music collaborations and in North–South Indian jugalbandi.
葛圖瓦賈姆琴可追溯至《Natya Shastra》（約公元前200年至公元200: The gottuvadyam can be traced to the seven-string fretless instrument described in the 《Natya Shastra》 (about 200 BC to AD 200), and it later appears in the 《Sangita Ratnakara》. At the end of the nineteenth and the beginning of the twentieth century Sakha Rama Rao named this Carnatic chordophone and brought it back to the concert platform. His pupil Gottuvadyam Narayana Iyengar was a court musician to the former Travancore and Mysore courts and raised the standing of its playing; his son Narasimhan carried on the elder generation's fingering, tuning and manner of playing. The instrument developed from the early seven strings into today's fretless construction of twenty or twenty-one strings resembling the South Indian veena; it is played mainly in South India and has entered world music and North–South Indian ensemble settings.
葛圖瓦賈姆琴的共鳴箱體主要採用木材製造，通常選用南印度的傳統樂器木材如黑檀木或紅: The resonator of the gottuvadyam is mainly made of wood, usually the traditional South Indian instrument woods such as ebony or rosewood. The neck and head are of hard wood as well. The strings are metal and have a metallic character. The bridge is of ivory, crystal or hardwood. The back has a leather or goatskin facing that strengthens the resonance. The tuning pegs and fittings are of metal or wood, combining traditional craft with practical performance.
葛圖瓦賈姆琴音色溫潤而富有歌唱性，兼具琵琶的清晰與維那琴的柔和特質。其音域寬廣，: The gottuvadyam has a warm, singing timbre, with both the clarity of the pipa and the softness of the veena. Its range is wide, covering the high, middle and low registers, and the colour changes with where the strings are played — near the bridge it is bright and penetrating, further away it turns dark and deep. The strings resonate warmly through the body, with good continuity and depth. Where a guitar sounds open and clear, the gottuvadyam has more of an Eastern character and more emotional range; beside the traditional veena its sound is more metallic and more modern. The unusual fretless design lets it make subtle changes of pitch, which suits the complex melodic rise and fall and the expression of Carnatic music.
